      <content name="altTitle">Privacy</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Patient</span> health record</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>You've probably seen your chart at your doctor's office. In fact, you may have charts at several doctors' offices.  If you've been in the hospital, you have a chart there, too. These charts are your medical records. They may be on paper or electronic. To keep track of all this information, it's a good idea to keep your own personal health record.  </p><p>What kind of information would you put in a personal health record? You could start with:</p><ul><li>	Your name, birth date, blood type, and emergency contact information</li><li>	Date of last physical</li><li>	Dates and results of tests and screenings</li><li>	Major illnesses and surgeries, with dates</li><li>	A list of your medicines and supplements, the dosages, and how long you've taken them</li><li>	Any allergies</li><li>	Any chronic diseases</li><li>	Any history of illnesses in your family</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/patientrights.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Patient</span> Rights</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Informed Consent</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ombudsman Programs</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Privacy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Second Opinion</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt0">patient</span> rights?<p>As a <span class="qt0">patient</span>, you have certain rights. Some are guaranteed by federal law, such as the right to get a copy of your medical records and the right to keep them private and secure. Many states have additional laws protecting <span class="qt0">patients</span>. And some states, insurance plans, medical organizations, and health care facilities have their own <span class="qt0">patient</span> bill of rights.</p><p>Some other examples of <span class="qt0">patient</span> rights include:</p><ul><li>Being treated with respect</li><li>Not being discriminated against in your medical care</li><li>The right to refuse treatment</li><li>The right of informed consent</li></ul>What is informed consent?<p>Informed consent is an important <span class="qt0">patient</span> right. It is a process in which your health care provider gives you the information you need to make decisions about your care. The types of care could be treatments, procedures, genetic testing, or clinical trials. The information should include the risks and benefits of the care, as well as details about your medical condition.</p><p>It's important that you understand everything before you give consent. Sometimes your provider will ask you to sign a form to give your consent. This is called written consent.</p><p>You have the right to change your mind about consent at any time.</p>Where can I get help with <span class="qt0">patient</span> rights?<p>There are different resources that can help you if you have a problem with your <span class="qt0">patient</span> rights:</p><ul><li>Many hospitals have <span class="qt0">patient</span> advocates. These are people who can help guide you through the health care system and make sure that your rights are protected.
</li><li>Your state may have resources to help you, such as: 
  <ul><li>Your state may have an office (called an ombudsmen office) for problems with long term care.</li><li>Your state's department of health may be able to help.</li><li>States also have oversight agencies for insurance companies and various types of health care facilities and providers. These agencies make sure that these organizations and providers follow the rules so you can get quality care.</li></ul>
</li><li>The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has an Office for Civil Rights (OCR). You can file a complaint with them if you feel you have been discriminated against in your medical care or if you think your health information privacy rights have been violated.</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/patientsafety.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Patient</span> Safety</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>You can help prevent medical errors by being an active member of your health care team. Research shows that <span class="qt0">patients</span> who are more involved with their care tend to get better results.  To reduce the risk of medical errors, you can:</p><ul><li>Ask questions if you have doubts or concerns. Take a relative or friend to your doctor appointment to help you ask questions and understand answers.</li><li>Make sure you understand what will happen if you need surgery</li><li>Tell your health care providers about all the medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and dietary supplements. Tell them if you have any allergies or bad reactions to anesthesia. Make sure you know how to take your medications correctly. </li><li>Get a second opinion about treatment options</li><li>Keep a copy of your own medical history</li></ul><p>Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/talkingwithyourdoctor.html">
      <content name="title">Talking With Your Doctor</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Communicating With Your Healthcare Provider</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Second Opinion</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Talk to Your Doctor</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>How well you and your doctor or provider communicate with each other is one of the most important parts of getting good health care. Being prepared can help you make the most of your visit, whether it is in person or through telehealth. Here are some things you can do to make the most of your appointment:</p><ul><li>Make lists of any allergies you have and all the medicines, herbs, vitamins, and supplements you take.</li><li>Make a list of the questions and concerns you want to talk about.</li><li>If you are having any health problems, write down a description of your symptoms. Include information such as when they started, what makes them better, and what makes them worse.</li><li>Ask a trusted friend or family member to come to the appointment with you.</li><li>If your doctor or provider doesn't speak your language, call their office ahead of time and ask them to provide an interpreter.</li><li>During your appointment, take notes about what your doctor or health care provider tells you. Or you could ask your friend or family member to take notes for you.</li><li>Be honest during your appointment. Don't just say what you think your doctor or provider wants to hear. For example, don't say that you stopped smoking or are eating healthy if it's not true. Your doctor or provider needs to know what is really going on, so they can give you the care and treatments that would be best for you.</li><li>If you don't understand something your doctor or provider says, ask questions until you do understand.</li><li>Ask for written instructions if you need them.</li><li>Learn how to access your medical records, so you can keep track of your test results, diagnoses, treatment plans, and medicines.</li><li>Ask for your doctor's or provider's contact information and find out the best way to communicate with them.</li><li>Find out what to do if you need more information later.</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/caregivers.html">
      <content name="title">Caregivers</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A caregiver gives care to someone who needs help taking care of themselves. The person who needs help may be a child, an adult, or an older adult. They may need help because of an injury or disability.  Or they may have a chronic illness such as Alzheimer's disease or cancer.</p><p>Some caregivers are informal caregivers. They are usually family members or friends. Other caregivers are paid professionals. Caregivers may give care at home or in a hospital or other health care setting. Sometimes they are caregiving from a distance. The types of tasks that caregivers do may include:</p><ul><li>Helping with daily tasks like bathing, eating, or taking medicine</li><li>Doing housework and cooking</li><li>Running errands such as shopping for food and clothes</li><li>Driving the person to appointments</li><li>Providing company and emotional support</li><li>Arranging activities and medical care</li><li>Making health and financial decisions</li></ul><p>Caregiving can be rewarding. It may help to strengthen connections to a loved one. You may feel fulfillment from helping someone else. But caregiving may also be stressful and sometimes even overwhelming. You may be "on call" for 24 hours a day. You may also be working outside the home and taking care of children. So you need to make sure that you are not ignoring your own needs. You have to take care of your own physical and mental health as well. Because when you feel better, you can take better care of your loved one. It will also be easier to focus on the rewards of caregiving.</p><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>
